nameStory: The 'royal' in royal catchfly refers to its magnificent bright red flowers that stand tall like a crown above the prairie grasses. The 'catchfly' name comes from the sticky stems that can trap small insects, though this trait is less pronounced in royal catchfly than in some of its relatives. It's truly the royalty of the prairie wildflower world!
description: Royal catchfly is a striking prairie wildflower that grows up to 5 feet tall from a deep, fleshy taproot. Its brilliant red tubular flowers bloom in clusters at the top of sturdy upright stems, creating a dramatic splash of color in late summer. The lance-shaped leaves start large at the base and get progressively smaller up the stem. This is an exceptionally rare plant in New England, with only a handful of sightings recorded.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright scarlet-red tubular flowers with 5 deeply notched petals that flare out from a long, narrow tube with 10 prominent veins running lengthwise - the tube feels firm and slightly sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall upright stems reaching 3-5 feet high, growing in small clumps from a deep taproot, with flowers clustered at the very top of each stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped to oval leaves up to 5 inches long that are arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, feeling smooth but slightly thick and succulent-like

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, somewhat sticky stems that may trap tiny insects - run your finger along the stem and you'll feel a slight tackiness

habitat: Royal catchfly is native to tallgrass prairie habitats and is extremely rare in New England, where it would be found in sunny, open grasslands or prairie remnants. In its native range, it grows in full sun in prairie openings, woodland edges, and sometimes along roadsides where prairie conditions persist. Any New England sighting would likely be in maintained grasslands, prairie restorations, or possibly escaped from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the deep taproot as the weather warms, with opposite leaves appearing along the developing stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in late summer, typically July through August, when the spectacular red flower clusters open at stem tips.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while the leaves may turn yellowish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to the ground, surviving as dormant taproots buried deep in the soil.

funFact: Royal catchfly flowers are specially designed for ruby-throated hummingbirds - the long red tubes perfectly match the length of a hummingbird's beak and tongue, making this one of the few New England wildflowers that depends entirely on hummingbirds rather than bees or butterflies for pollination!
confusionNotes: Royal catchfly could be confused with fire pink (Silene virginica), but royal catchfly is much taller (3-5 feet vs 1-2 feet), has larger flower clusters, and blooms later in summer rather than spring. The tube of royal catchfly is also notably longer and more prominently veined.
contextualKnowledge: Royal catchfly is native to the American Midwest's tallgrass prairie and is considered extirpated or extremely rare throughout most of its range due to prairie habitat loss. Any New England sightings are likely garden escapes or intentional prairie restoration plantings rather than truly wild populations.
compareHints: Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time. Fire pink blooms in spring and stays much shorter, while red campion has smaller, less tubular flowers. Royal catchfly's flowers have the longest tubes in the genus, perfectly sized for hummingbird beaks rather than the shorter tubes adapted for butterflies or moths.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
